Non-functional requirements

Targets, constraints and evidence obligations — how experienced practitioners price a quality, where the arithmetic bites, and the disagreements the field has never settled.

1 · Two roomsThe same topic, two different crises

On the morning of 9 February 2026, Sarayu Iyengar was handed a two-page annexure and asked to say yes or no by Friday. Sarayu is VP of Product at Amodini Health Systems, a Hyderabad company that sells a hospital information system — registration, orders, pharmacy, billing, discharge — to mid-sized Indian hospital groups. The annexure had come from the procurement office of a fourteen-hospital chain in Maharashtra and Gujarat that was about to sign a three-year contract worth roughly ₹31 crore, the largest in Amodini's history. It was not a feature list. It was a schedule of qualities: 99.99 per cent monthly availability with service credits, patient-record retrieval in under one second at the ninety-fifth percentile during the 8 to 11 a.m. outpatient peak, a complete and immutable audit trail of every access to every record, storage and processing of patient data only on infrastructure located in India, and recovery from a data-centre loss within fifteen minutes.

Amodini's own engineering had measured 99.93 per cent availability over the previous twelve months and a p95 record-retrieval time of 1.9 seconds at peak. The sales director wanted the annexure signed as written, on the reasoning that everybody signs these and nobody reads them again. Sarayu's platform architect, Bhaskar Menon, had estimated that the availability clause alone implied an active-active deployment across two Indian regions, costing about ₹1.4 crore a year in infrastructure and two additional on-call engineers. The contract's own penalty schedule, meanwhile, capped credits at 10 per cent of the quarterly fee. Sarayu was being asked to buy ₹1.4 crore of insurance against a liability that could not exceed ₹8.6 lakh a quarter.

Eight days later and 700 kilometres away, Kabir Anand faced a problem with the same shape and none of the same vocabulary. Kabir is head of product at Ambarika Play, a Mumbai company whose app streams audiobooks, devotional recitations and serialised fiction in eleven Indian languages to about 4.1 crore monthly active users, two-thirds of them outside the eight largest cities. On 17 February 2026 his team demonstrated an AI narration feature: a publisher uploads a manuscript in Marathi or Bhojpuri and the system generates a narrated audiobook in a chosen voice, collapsing a production cycle that currently takes six weeks and about ₹1.1 lakh per title into something that takes an afternoon.

The demonstration was excellent. The requirements document was not. It said the feature must be “fast, cost-effective and high quality”. When Kabir asked what quality meant, the answer was that the narration should not mispronounce words. When he asked how many mispronunciations were acceptable, the room went quiet, because nobody had considered that the answer might not be zero, and nobody knew how they would count. Ambarika Play's board had approved the feature on an assumption of ₹180 per generated hour of audio against ₹9,000 per hour for studio recording — a number that depended entirely on how many times each chapter had to be regenerated, which depended entirely on a quality bar that did not yet exist.

Both executives were dealing with non-functional requirements. Sarayu's were over-specified, expensively, by someone else. Kabir's were unspecified, dangerously, by his own team. The argument of this page is that these are the same failure — a failure to distinguish qualities you choose and pay for from qualities imposed on you and proved to others — and that the remedy in both cases is arithmetic rather than adjectives.

2 · The idea and its schoolsWhat the term means, and who disagrees about it

A functional requirement specifies what a system must do: an input, a state, an output. A non-functional requirement — equivalently a quality requirement or quality attribute — specifies a property the system must exhibit while doing it: how quickly, how reliably, how securely, at what scale, under which jurisdiction, in whose language, on whose hardware, and with what evidence available afterwards. The distinction is old and, as we will see, contested.

Its intellectual history runs through three traditions. The first is quality modelling: Barry Boehm's 1976 characteristics tree, which argued that “quality” decomposes into attributes that can conflict, and its institutional descendants ISO/IEC 9126 and ISO/IEC 25010, which give the field its standard vocabulary of performance efficiency, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, compatibility and usability. The second is software architecture: the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon, and in particular Len Bass, Paul Clements and Rick Kazman's Software Architecture in Practice, which made the operational claim that quality attributes — not functions — determine architecture, and supplied the six-part quality attribute scenario (source, stimulus, artefact, environment, response, response measure) together with the Architecture Tradeoff Analysis Method for eliciting and ranking them. The third is measurement: Tom Gilb's Planguage, which insists that every quality carries a scale and a meter and a set of levels, and, more recently, the site-reliability practice popularised by Google's 2016 book, which converts reliability into a service-level objective with an explicit error budget — a quantified permission to fail, owned jointly by the teams that cause failures and the teams that suffer them.

Competent practitioners genuinely disagree, and it is worth stating the schools by the proposition each would sign.

The architecture school signs: qualities must be elicited before the architecture is chosen, because they determine structure and cannot be retrofitted. It refuses the proposition that non-functionals can be deferred to a hardening phase. Its evidence is the long record of systems that could not be made fast or secure later at any price.

The quantification school signs: a quality without a scale and a meter is not a requirement but a wish, and should be struck from the document. It refuses the proposition that some qualities are inherently unquantifiable. Gilb's position is that “unquantifiable” always means “we have not yet decided what we would measure”.

The error-budget school signs two propositions the others find uncomfortable: the correct reliability target is the point at which users stop noticing, and anything beyond that is waste; and the residual unreliability should be spent deliberately, on release velocity. It refuses the proposition that higher availability is always better. Its evidence is cost curves: the marginal price of each additional nine rises faster than the marginal user benefit.

The integrationist school — Suzanne and James Robertson's Volere approach, and in a sharper form the critique that the functional/non-functional split is philosophically incoherent because every quality is ultimately observable behaviour — signs: attach a fit criterion to every requirement and abolish the separate non-functional annex. It refuses the proposition that qualities deserve their own document. Its evidence is the annex nobody reads.

The softgoal school, associated with Lawrence Chung and John Mylopoulos and borrowing Herbert Simon's notion of satisficing, signs: many qualities are not thresholds but goals that are satisficed to a degree, and are best modelled as a network of positive and negative contributions, because improving one degrades another. It refuses the proposition that every quality reduces to a single number.

The assurance school — the auditors, and everyone who has survived an ISO 27001 or SOC 2 cycle or a regulator's inspection — signs: some requirements are evidence obligations rather than performance targets; what matters is not only that the property holds but that you can prove it held, eleven months later, to someone hostile. It refuses the proposition that controls may be traded against velocity.

The practical synthesis available to Sarayu and Kabir is not a reconciliation of these schools but a sorting rule. Every candidate requirement is one of three things: a target the organisation chooses and pays for, tradeable; a constraint imposed by law, physics or contract, binary; or an evidence obligation, which is satisfied only by a durable record. The three behave differently in prioritisation, in verification and in what happens when they are missed, and most organisational confusion comes from treating one as another.

3 · Mechanics in depthUtility trees, budgets and the arithmetic underneath

Sarayu's first move was not to negotiate the annexure but to build what the SEI tradition calls a utility tree: a decomposition of “utility” into quality attributes, then into concrete scenarios, each rated twice — once for importance to the business, once for difficulty of achievement. The double rating is the point. It concentrates attention on the small number of scenarios that are both high-importance and high-difficulty, which are precisely the scenarios that will shape the architecture and consume the budget.

The second move is to convert each surviving scenario into a budget rather than a wish. A latency target decomposes across the hops of a journey; an availability target decomposes across the services in a dependency chain; a cost target decomposes across the units of work. The decomposition is where most teams discover that the number they wrote is impossible, which is the useful outcome.

Two pieces of arithmetic do most of the work, and both are routinely skipped. The first is composition of availability in series. If a clinician's record-retrieval journey touches five services, each independently achieving 99.9 per cent, the journey's availability is not 99.9 per cent but 0.999 raised to the fifth power, which is 0.99501 — 99.50 per cent, or about 3 hours 39 minutes of failure a month rather than 43 minutes. The architectural consequences follow immediately: either the components must be better, or some of them must be removed from the critical path, or the journey must degrade gracefully rather than fail. That third option is the interesting one, because it converts an availability requirement into a functional requirement — what does the screen show when the billing service is unreachable? — and functional requirements are far cheaper to satisfy than nines.

The second is the relationship between utilisation and tail latency. Under the standard single-queue approximation, the average time a request spends in a system — waiting plus being served — is the service time divided by one minus the utilisation. At 50 per cent utilisation a request takes twice its service time; at 80 per cent, five times; at 90 per cent, ten times; at 95 per cent, twenty times. The curve does not bend gently. It is the reason a system that looks comfortable on average falls over at the peak, and the reason a demanding percentile target is really a statement about how much idle capacity the business is willing to pay for.

The arithmetic behind those three points is worth following. At the outpatient peak, roughly 4,200 clinicians are logged in, each issuing a request about every twenty seconds, giving an arrival rate of 4,200 ÷ 20 = 210 requests per second. Each node handles 25 requests per second. Eleven nodes give capacity of 275 per second, a utilisation of 210 ÷ 275 = 0.76, and a response time of about 40 ÷ (1 − 0.76) = 167 milliseconds, which Bhaskar rounded to 200 for safety. Fourteen nodes give capacity of 350, a utilisation of 0.60, and about 100 milliseconds. Ten nodes give capacity of 250, a utilisation of 0.84, and 250 milliseconds on average — but averages are not the promise, and at that utilisation the ninety-fifth percentile stretched past 400 milliseconds in load tests. Three additional nodes cost Amodini approximately ₹14 lakh a year. Measured against a one-second browser-side target of which the server is only one component, that is the cheapest clause in the annexure.

The step practitioners leave implicit sits between the target and the budget: naming the measurement point. The hospital's annexure said “patient record retrieval under one second”. Amodini measured at the application load balancer, where the figure was 190 milliseconds. The hospital's clinicians measured with a stopwatch on a shared workstation in an OPD corridor, where the figure was 1.9 seconds, most of it browser rendering of a 340-row order history and a network that traversed the hospital's own wired estate. Both parties had been right and neither had been talking to the other, because the requirement omitted the only clause that would have forced the conversation.

4 · When it applies, and when it misleads

The discipline is not universally valuable, and it is worth stating the conditions as claims that can be tested against a specific situation rather than as advice.

Claim one: the quality must be capable of failing in a way someone would notice. Applied to Amodini, availability passes trivially — a hospital that cannot retrieve a record at 9 a.m. notices within seconds. Applied to Ambarika Play's narration feature, time-to-first-audio passes, but “maintainability of the generation pipeline” does not: nobody outside the team would ever observe it, so writing it as a requirement produces an unfalsifiable clause. Maintainability belongs in engineering practice, not in a quality contract with a meter.

Claim two: the quality must be measurable at a point both parties accept before the argument starts. Amodini's retrieval time fails this test as written and passes once the measurement moves into the browser. Kabir's mispronunciation rate fails it at first glance — who decides what counts as a mispronunciation in Bhojpuri? — and passes only once he commissions a fixed panel of three language reviewers with an adjudication rule, which is a real cost and must be budgeted as part of the requirement.

Claim three: the cost curve must have a knee the organisation can locate. Availability has one; Sarayu could point to it. Security does not, in the same clean way: there is no utilisation-style curve that tells you when you have bought enough defence, which is why the assurance school's evidence-obligation framing serves better there than the target framing.

The idea becomes actively misleading in two situations. The first is when a quality target substitutes for a decision about what the product is. A team that spends a quarter taking p95 from 900 to 600 milliseconds on a screen nobody wants has satisfied a requirement and wasted a quarter; the requirement document contains no mechanism to notice. The second is when quality targets are set for a system whose behaviour is probabilistic. A deterministic system either meets a latency bound or does not; a generative system produces a distribution of outputs, and a threshold on that distribution is only meaningful alongside a sampling plan. Writing “narration must be accurate” in the same register as “the page must load in two seconds” imports a false sense of verifiability, and this is precisely the trap Ambarika Play walked into.

5 · Hard edgesSeams, two-sided systems, hardware and AI

Multi-product companies discover that quality requirements are the main thing that does not compose across a portfolio. Amodini sells its hospital system alongside a lightweight clinic product and a patient app; the three share an identity service. The identity service inherits the strictest availability requirement of any consumer, which means the clinic product's undemanding customers are subsidising the hospital chain's nines, and the patient app's traffic spikes threaten the hospital's tail latency. The honest response is not a single system-wide number but per-tenant isolation with separate budgets — and the discovery that quality requirements are an argument about shared infrastructure economics wearing an engineering costume.

Two-sided systems generate qualities that have no single-user analogue. Amodit Freight Exchange, a Chennai marketplace matching shippers with truck operators, found that its most important non-functional requirement was not latency or uptime but staleness symmetry: no two carriers may see the same load as available for more than 400 milliseconds after one of them accepts it, because a carrier who repeatedly loses races stops bidding. That is a requirement about the relationship between users, verifiable only by instrumenting pairs of sessions. Marketplace practitioners eventually build a vocabulary for these — fairness, consistency of match, bounded staleness — that the ISO catalogue does not contain.

Regulated contexts convert targets into evidence obligations. Under the Digital Personal Data Protection Act and the health-data architecture emerging around the Ayushman Bharat Digital Mission, it is not enough for Amodini to restrict access to patient records; it must be able to produce, on request, the consent artefact that authorised each access, months later, in a form an auditor accepts. The engineering implication is a write path that cannot be skipped under load — which conflicts directly with the latency target, because an append-only audit write on the critical path adds milliseconds to every read. This is what the SEI literature calls a tradeoff point: a decision that cannot be optimised for one attribute without degrading another, and which therefore belongs to a named human rather than to a coding standard.

Hardware-plus-software situations add qualities that pure software teams never confront, chiefly because bits must reach devices the company does not control. Amoda Instruments, a Coimbatore maker of connected point-of-care diagnostic analysers, had an impeccable cloud availability record and a fleet in which a third of devices ran firmware more than two versions old. Its quality contract had no clause about update convergence, because nobody had thought of the fleet as a system with a quality.

AI-native features add a third register again. Ambarika Play's narration pipeline has conventional qualities — time to first audio, cost per generated hour, throughput at publisher-upload peaks — and one that behaves unlike anything in the classical catalogue: output quality, which is statistical, contested, and drifts when an underlying model changes without warning. The right treatment borrows from manufacturing rather than from software: an acceptance sampling plan with a defined sample size, a defined defect definition, an adjudication procedure and a control chart. It also requires a clause almost nobody writes: a statement of what happens when the supplier changes the model, since a quality established by measurement on one model version is not inherited by the next.

At organisational seams, the general pattern is that quality requirements fail where ownership changes hands. The platform team owns the latency budget; feature teams spend it; and unless the budget is enforced in the build pipeline — a failing check when a payload exceeds its cap, a blocked deploy when the error budget is exhausted — it is advisory, and advisory budgets are always overspent. Mature companies say they manage this with governance. What they actually do is automate the refusal.

6 · Nuances that separate expert from competent

The expert asks where the measurement is taken before asking what the number is

The tell is a question about instrumentation in the first thirty seconds of a performance conversation. The obvious reading — that the number is the substance and the instrument is detail — is wrong, because the instrument determines which system is being described. Amodini's 190 milliseconds and the hospital's 1.9 seconds differed by an order of magnitude and neither party was mistaken.

The expert quotes percentiles per journey, not per endpoint

The tell is a dashboard organised by user flow rather than by service. A journey of eight sequential calls, each independently meeting a ninety-fifth-percentile target, delivers a clean session only 0.95 to the eighth power of the time — about 66 per cent. Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Barroso made this argument about tail latency at scale in 2013: as fan-out grows, the tail becomes the common experience. The naive reading, that meeting p95 everywhere means 95 per cent of users are happy, is arithmetically false.

The expert treats graceful degradation as the cheapest nine

The tell is the question “what does the screen show when this dependency is down?” asked during design rather than during an incident. Raising a component from 99.9 to 99.99 per cent is an architecture project; removing it from the critical path, or rendering a cached version with a visible staleness marker, is usually a fortnight. The obvious reading — that availability is bought with redundancy — misses that it is more often bought with product design.

The expert distinguishes targets, constraints and evidence obligations, and never scores the last two

The tell is a prioritisation exercise from which compliance items have been deliberately excluded, with a written note saying why. Ranking a legal obligation against a feature produces spreadsheets in which the obligation sits fourteenth and everyone feels the process was rigorous. The converse tell is equally diagnostic: an expert will happily renegotiate a self-chosen availability target in public, which practitioners who have sanctified their own numbers find shocking.

The expert knows the cost curve is stepwise, not smooth

The tell is an answer of the form “the next nine is not more servers, it is a different data architecture”. Qualities improve cheaply within an architecture and then hit a wall; the wall is where the product decision lives. Sarayu's ₹14 lakh for three nodes and ₹1.4 crore for a second active region are on opposite sides of one such wall.

The expert prices the target against the actual liability

The tell is arithmetic on the penalty schedule. Amodini's contract exposes at most 10 per cent of a quarterly fee, roughly ₹8.6 lakh. If historical performance suggests the 99.9 per cent threshold is breached in perhaps one quarter in six, the expected annual credit is about 4 × (1/6) × ₹8.6 lakh, or ₹5.7 lakh — against ₹1.4 crore a year to eliminate it. The reputational and renewal risks are real and not captured by that sum, which is the honest counter-argument; but an executive who has not done the arithmetic cannot have the conversation at all.

The expert puts an expiry date on every target

The tell is a review date in the requirement itself. Targets are set against a traffic profile, a device mix and a competitive landscape, all of which move. A payload cap calibrated for 3G in 2024 becomes an unnecessary product constraint once the median user is on 4G, and a p95 that was generous in 2023 becomes embarrassing once a competitor is faster. Requirements without expiry dates are not maintained; they are simply obeyed until someone notices they are absurd.

The expert treats perceptibility as part of the target

The tell is a refusal to fund an improvement. Human perception of latency is not linear: the difference between five seconds and two is transformative, between 900 milliseconds and 700 usually invisible. The naive reading is that faster is always better and the only question is cost. The expert's reading is that the value of a quality improvement is a step function with thresholds, and that the work is to find which side of a threshold the product currently sits on.

The expert demands a sampling plan for probabilistic qualities

The tell is a question about sample size. If Kabir's target is a mispronunciation rate below 0.25 per cent of words, and the weekly audit reviews 300 words, the expected number of defects in a clean sample is 0.75 — a measurement that cannot distinguish 0.25 per cent from 0.8 per cent. The standard approximation for the margin of error at 95 per cent confidence is 1.96 times the square root of p(1−p)/n. At p = 0.0025 and n = 4,000, that is about 0.155 percentage points, so the estimate reads “0.25 per cent, plus or minus 0.16”. At n = 20,000 words — roughly two hours of narration — it tightens to about 0.07 points. The requirement is therefore not one clause but two: a rate, and the audit volume that makes the rate knowable.

The expert names the tradeoff, not the attribute

The tell is a document that contains sentences of the form “we accept X in exchange for Y, decided by Z on this date”. Encryption at rest versus range-query performance; data residency versus cross-region failover; audit-write completeness versus read latency; strict rate limits versus partner integration convenience. Competent practitioners list attributes. Experts list the pairs that fight, because those pairs are where the architecture is actually decided.

7 · Across product types and stages

In consumer products the binding qualities live in the user's physical world: device class, network, battery, data cost, app size and language. Localisation is a genuine quality requirement rather than a translation task, since Devanagari strings run 20 to 35 per cent longer than their English equivalents and Indian digit grouping writes ₹12,34,567 where a Western locale writes 1,234,567; a layout that has not been pseudo-translation tested will break before it is misunderstood. Ambarika Play discovered that its most expensive non-functional constraint was the installed app size, because a 40-megabyte increase measurably depressed install completion on entry-level devices in Tier-3 towns.

In enterprise B2B the binding qualities arrive from outside: uptime with service credits, single sign-on, role-based access control, data export, audit trails, and a security questionnaire that functions as a requirements document authored by someone else's procurement team. The discipline here is commercial as much as technical — the time to discover a quality obligation is before the contract, and the artefact that prevents disaster is a published list of what the company does and does not commit to, so that a salesperson cannot invent a nine.

Platforms and marketplaces add the relational qualities described earlier, and one more that is easy to miss: for a platform, backward compatibility is a quality requirement with a scale and a meter — how long a deprecated interface remains available, how much notice partners receive — and it is routinely treated as a matter of courtesy instead.

Hardware adds fleet-level qualities: update convergence, offline tolerance, field-failure rate and the cost of a truck roll. AI products add statistical output qualities and a supplier-change clause. And in one respect all of them are the same, which is worth saying plainly rather than manufacturing a distinction: the sorting rule — target, constraint, evidence obligation — and the demand for a scale, a meter and an environment apply identically in every one of these contexts.

Stage changes the economics rather than the concepts. A company of fifteen people should hold three explicit quality requirements, chosen because violating them would be fatal or illegal, and should consciously accept debt everywhere else; writing eleven is a way of writing none. A company of Amodini's size has the opposite problem: its quality requirements are the only thing keeping shared infrastructure habitable across product lines, which means they must be owned centrally, budgeted, and enforced by machinery rather than by memo.

Unless renewal genuinely turns on it, the row does not survive the arithmetic.

The second example is Kabir's. Ambarika Play's board case rested on ₹180 per generated hour of audio. The underlying model call costs about ₹95 per hour of output. If 20 per cent of chapters must be regenerated once because of a pronunciation defect, the effective cost is 95 × 1.20 = ₹114. If the regeneration rate is 60 per cent and 15 per cent of those need a second pass, it is 95 × (1 + 0.60 + 0.09) = ₹160.55, and once human review time is added at ₹340 per hour of audio for a reviewer covering four hours of output per working hour — ₹85 per generated hour — the total reaches ₹245, well past the board's number and past the point where the business case narrows sharply against studio recording at ₹9,000. The quality requirement and the unit economics are the same object seen from two sides: the acceptable defect rate is whatever rate keeps the regeneration multiplier low enough for the cost target to hold. Kabir's first useful act was to stop asking what quality bar was right and start asking what regeneration rate the ₹180 figure could tolerate, which turned out to be about 0.35 passes per chapter.

The third example is the one that failed. Amoda Instruments shipped its connected analysers with an exemplary quality contract covering cloud availability, API latency, encryption and data residency, and met every clause for two years running — 99.97 per cent availability, p95 API latency of 140 milliseconds. In November 2025 a reagent-calibration correction had to reach the fleet. Thirty-one days after release, 67 per cent of the 2,800 installed analysers were running it. The remainder sat in clinics on 2G-class connectivity where the 14-megabyte firmware image, downloaded without resumption, failed repeatedly. No clause in the contract had ever described the fleet as a system; every clause described the servers.

The recovery is instructive because it was not an engineering heroics story. Amoda added one requirement — 95 per cent of the installed fleet runs the current firmware within 21 days of release, measured by device check-in telemetry — and then let the requirement force the design. Meeting it required delta updates, which reduced the typical image from 14 megabytes to about 900 kilobytes; resumable, chunked transfer; and a staged rollout with automatic rollback. Convergence at 21 days moved from 67 to 96 per cent over the following two quarters. The lesson the company drew was not that it needed better engineers but that its quality contract had described the wrong system, and that no amount of rigour inside a boundary compensates for drawing the boundary in the wrong place.

9 · Failure modes and their early warnings

The boilerplate annex. The early warning is textual identity: the same four sentences about performance, security and scale appear in every PRD. The diagnostic question is “which of these would have blocked last quarter's release?” Caught early it costs an hour; caught late it costs a pilot, because the team believed it had requirements and had only paragraphs.

The unpriced nine. The early warning is a number in a document that no engineer has been asked to cost. The diagnostic is to request the marginal cost of the last nine; if nobody can produce it, the number was never a commitment. Caught late, the cost is either a contractual liability nobody budgeted or a year of infrastructure spending defending a promise no customer required.

Verification scheduled after code-complete. The early warning is calendrical: the load test, penetration test and privacy review all sit in release week. The diagnostic is to look for any quality activity dated before the first line of production code. Caught late, the cost is architectural rework, which is the most expensive category of rework there is.

Compliance believed rather than evidenced. The early warning is a team that answers a compliance question by describing a screen. The diagnostic is to trace one named user's consent withdrawal end to end and ask who could prove it eleven months later. Caught late, the cost is a regulatory finding or a failed audit during a funding or acquisition process, at the worst possible moment.

Quality targets without an enforcing mechanism. The early warning is a budget that lives in a document rather than in the build pipeline. The diagnostic is to ask what automatically happens when a team exceeds the payload cap or burns the error budget; if the answer is a conversation, the budget is advisory. Caught late, the cost is gradual: the target erodes by a few per cent per release until it is quietly restated.

Targets that outlived their environment. The early warning is a requirement with no review date and a rationale nobody present can explain. The diagnostic is to ask what device mix, traffic profile or competitor the number was set against. Caught late, the cost is usually invisible — engineering effort spent defending a constraint that stopped mattering two years ago.

10 · Where experts genuinely disagree

Annex or inline. One camp holds that quality requirements belong in a dedicated, owned section of the specification, because they are cross-cutting, because they need a named owner, and because scattering them into user stories guarantees that no one ever sees the system-level picture. The other holds, with the fit-criteria tradition, that a separate annex is where requirements go to die, and that a quality attached to the story a developer picks up on Monday is the only kind that gets built. Each position rests on real evidence: the first on systems that were architecturally incoherent because nobody held the whole, the second on the observably unread appendix. The first would be wrong if teams reliably read annexes, which they do not; the second would be wrong if cross-cutting qualities could be decomposed without loss into individual stories, which they cannot. Most experienced practitioners run both and feel slightly guilty about the duplication.

Whether error budgets are a real currency. The steelman for the practice is that reliability and velocity are genuinely in tension, that making the tension explicit and quantified moves the argument from status to arithmetic, and that a freeze triggered automatically by budget exhaustion is the only mechanism anyone has found that actually stops a shipping organisation. The steelman against is structural: the mechanism works where the team that suffers unreliability is organisationally distinct from the team that causes it, and in a company where the same director owns both, an error budget is a number that director may override, which makes it theatre. The disagreement is not about the arithmetic but about whether the organisation can bind itself. It would be settled against the practice if budgets were shown to be overridden in most organisations that adopt them, which nobody has measured properly.

Whether security can be expressed as requirements at all. The control-list position holds that enumerable obligations — encryption at rest, least privilege, log retention, patch windows — are necessary, auditable and the only thing that scales across a large engineering organisation. The threat-modelling position holds that a control list describes what you decided to defend and is silent about what an adversary will attempt, and that treating security as a requirements problem produces compliant systems that are breached. The strongest version of each is compatible with the other in principle and rarely in budget, since both consume the same scarce security engineers.

Whether AI output quality is a non-functional requirement. One position says yes: it is a quality with a scale, a meter and a threshold, precisely like latency, differing only in requiring statistical measurement. The other says no: for a generative feature, output quality is the function — it is what the user bought — and demoting it to an annex is how teams end up shipping features that work and are worthless. This one is live and unsettled, and Kabir's team argued about it for a fortnight without resolution.

Perception-anchored versus competition-anchored targets. The first says set the target where users stop noticing and spend the surplus elsewhere. The second says users notice comparatively, not absolutely, so the relevant threshold is the fastest credible alternative, which moves. Both are defensible; they diverge sharply in categories where a well-funded competitor is actively buying speed.

11 · What mastery looks like

Someone who has internalised this topic behaves differently in four observable ways. First, they ask for the measurement point before the number, and they will not discuss a target until the environment clause exists. Second, they price qualities out loud, in currency, and treat a target as a purchase rather than an aspiration — which means they will argue publicly for a lower number when the arithmetic supports it, a move that people who have merely studied the topic find uncomfortable. Third, they sort ruthlessly into targets, constraints and evidence obligations, and they never allow a legal obligation into a prioritisation score or a self-chosen target out of one. Fourth, and most tellingly, they write fewer quality requirements than the novice, not more: three to six per feature, each with an owner, a meter, a verification date and an expiry, and nothing at all where they have consciously decided to accept the risk. The novice's document is longer, more responsible-sounding, and produces no decisions.

12 · What they decided

Sarayu did not sign the annexure as written. She countered with 99.95 per cent availability, a defined read-only degraded mode with its own thirty-second target, and a one-second retrieval target explicitly measured in the browser on a specified workstation configuration in a named hospital, with a joint quarterly measurement review. She accepted the residency and audit clauses without negotiation, because they were constraints and evidence obligations rather than targets, and she attached the ₹14 lakh of additional nodes to the deal rather than the ₹1.4 crore. The hospital's procurement office accepted after four weeks, and the deciding argument was not the price but the measurement clause: for the first time, both parties knew what would count as failure.

Kabir inverted his problem. Rather than set a quality bar and hope the economics followed, he derived the bar from the economics — a regeneration rate of 0.35 passes per chapter — and then commissioned a sampling plan capable of measuring it: 20,000 words per language per week, three reviewers with an adjudication rule, a defect taxonomy separating mispronunciation from prosody from outright substitution, and a standing clause that any change to the underlying model resets the measurement rather than inheriting it. He launched in three languages instead of eleven, because the audit cost scales with languages and the sampling plan, not the model, was the binding constraint.

Discussion questions. First: Sarayu priced availability against a capped contractual liability and concluded that 99.99 per cent was not worth ₹1.4 crore. Under what circumstances would that arithmetic be the wrong way to frame the decision, and what evidence would you want before overriding it? Second: Kabir derived his quality bar from a unit-cost target rather than from any judgement about what listeners deserve. Is that a disciplined use of non-functional requirements or an abdication of product judgement — and what would the alternative procedure actually look like? Third: Amoda Instruments met every clause in its quality contract while a third of its fleet ran obsolete firmware. What is the general procedure for discovering that your quality contract describes the wrong system, and when in a product's life should it be run?

13 · Going deeper

  1. PRD structure. The document that holds all of this. Quality requirements only function when they sit somewhere with an owner and a review cadence; learning where they belong in a specification determines whether they are read.
  2. Compliance and audit requirements. The natural next step, because it takes the third category — evidence obligations — and treats it properly: retention, provability, reportability and the machinery that makes a claim defensible to an auditor rather than merely true.
  3. PM artefacts: one-pager, PRD, spec, strategy doc. Different artefacts carry different qualities. Knowing which document is the right home for an availability target versus a data-residency constraint prevents the annex problem described in section ten.
  4. Writing a one-pager. The discipline of compression is where the target-versus-constraint sorting proves itself: a one-pager has room for three qualities, which forces the choice this topic is about.
  5. Customer narratives (Day 0 / Day N). Quality requirements are usually discovered by imagining the system on a bad day rather than a good one; Day N narratives are the most reliable elicitation technique for the scenarios that populate a utility tree.
  6. Acceptance criteria and error cases. Where the feature-local half of this topic lands in the stories developers actually pick up, and where graceful degradation stops being an architecture idea and becomes a screen someone designs.
  7. Telemetry requirements. No quality requirement is real without the instrument that measures it; telemetry is the meter, and specifying it is part of specifying the requirement rather than a downstream engineering task.
  8. Release criteria and success metrics. The final gate: deciding which of these promises actually blocks a launch, which merely informs it, and how the organisation behaves when a target is missed on the morning of a release.

Delivery & Technology · Requirements & Specification

Non-functional requirements

What the feature must also be — fast enough, secure enough, lawful, legible in the user's language — and why the sentence “the system must be performant and scalable” has never once changed an engineering decision.

1 · The pilotA feature that worked perfectly and still failed

On 3 March 2026, Meghana Sule sat in the Kalyani Nagar office of Ambarish Money in Pune with two numbers in front of her that refused to reconcile. Ambarish Money is a consumer lending app: it originates small personal loans, typically between ₹15,000 and ₹2 lakh, in partnership with a non-banking financial company that holds the credit risk. The app had roughly 62 lakh installs, about ₹1,850 crore of loans outstanding, and a product organisation of nine people, of whom Meghana was the director.

The feature in question was a self-service foreclosure flow — the ability for a borrower to see the exact amount needed to close a loan early, including accrued interest and charges, and pay it in one step without calling the collections desk. Functionally it was finished. Every acceptance criterion in the PRD passed. In the four-week pilot across Pune, Nashik and Nagpur, it had been used 11,400 times, and the money had arrived correctly on every occasion.

The second number was the problem. On devices priced below ₹12,000 — roughly 46 per cent of Ambarish Money's active base — 34 per cent of borrowers who opened the foreclosure screen abandoned it before the amount rendered. The screen was not broken. It was slow: on a congested 3G cell in Nagpur at 8 p.m. it took between five and seven seconds to paint. Rohit Kannan, who ran the platform group, had measured the server side and found a median response time of 240 milliseconds, which he considered excellent, and which was true and irrelevant.

Meghana reread the PRD. Under a heading called Non-functional requirements sat four sentences she recognised from every other PRD the team had written that year: the system must be performant; the system must be secure; the system must scale; the system must comply with applicable regulations. Nafisa Sheikh, the compliance head, had signed it. Nobody had lied. Nobody had been lazy, exactly. But the section had made no claim that anyone could have failed, and so nobody had failed it, and so a finished feature was quietly losing a third of its users. Meghana had eleven weeks before the vernacular rollout into Tier-3 towns, which would add Marathi and Hindi interfaces and a device mix poorer still. She had to decide what, precisely, to write instead.

2 · The ideaRequirements about qualities, not about functions

A functional requirement states what the system must do: given this input and this state, produce this output. A non-functional requirement — also called a quality requirement, a quality attribute, or, in older engineering shorthand, an “-ility” — states a property the system must exhibit while doing it: how fast, how reliably, how securely, at what scale, under what law, in whose language, on whose hardware. Ambarish Money's foreclosure flow satisfied every functional requirement and violated a non-functional one that had never been written down.

The idea has a traceable history. Barry Boehm's 1976 work on quantitative software quality proposed a tree of quality characteristics rather than a single notion of “good”. The international standard now known as ISO/IEC 25010 organises those characteristics into a product-quality model — performance efficiency, reliability, security, maintainability, portability, compatibility, usability, functional suitability — which is useful chiefly as a checklist for remembering what you forgot. The operationally important contribution came from the Software Engineering Institute at Carnegie Mellon in the late 1990s, in the book Software Architecture in Practice by Len Bass, Paul Clements and Rick Kazman: qualities should be expressed as quality attribute scenarios, six-part statements naming a source, a stimulus, an artefact, an environment, a response and a response measure. In parallel, Tom Gilb argued in his Planguage notation that any quality claim without a scale and a measuring instrument is not a requirement but a wish. More recently, Google's site-reliability engineering practice reframed availability as a service-level objective with an error budget: a quantified allowance of failure that the organisation is permitted — in fact expected — to spend.

The sentence Meghana could repeat in a meeting without sounding glib was this: a non-functional requirement is a promise about a quality, stated with a number, a measurement point and an environment, such that it is possible to fail it. The test of an NFR is not whether it sounds responsible. The test is whether a reasonable engineer could look at the system and say, with evidence, that the promise was broken.

3 · How it actually worksTwo questions before any number

Before writing targets, an experienced practitioner sorts candidate qualities along two axes, because the two axes imply completely different treatment. The first axis asks whether the requirement is a target you have chosen — tradeable against cost and time, and therefore a product decision — or a constraint imposed from outside by regulation, contract or physics, which is binary and not yours to negotiate. The second axis asks whether the requirement belongs to this feature alone or is cross-cutting, holding across the whole system so that every future feature inherits it.

Having sorted them, the practitioner writes each one as a scenario rather than an adjective. The six parts are worth learning because each one, omitted, is a place where the requirement later dissolves. Source: who or what triggers the behaviour — a borrower, a collections agent, a partner bank's reconciliation job. Stimulus: the specific event. Artefact: which part of the system is on the hook. Environment: the conditions, which for Indian consumer products means device class, network, time of day and language. Response: the observable behaviour. Response measure: the number, the unit, the percentile and — the step almost everyone leaves implicit — the point in the stack where the measurement is taken.

That last omission is exactly what defeated Ambarish Money. Rohit's 240 milliseconds was a server-side measurement taken at the application load balancer. The borrower in Nagpur experiences a client-side measurement taken from the moment her thumb leaves the screen to the moment she can read a number. The two quantities were both real and had almost nothing to do with each other. A performance requirement that does not name its measurement point is not a weak requirement; it is not a requirement at all, because two honest people can both claim compliance.

The remaining steps are quick to state and rarely done. Give each scenario three levels rather than one: the must, below which you will not ship; the plan, which you commit to; and the wish, which you would take if it were cheap. Name an owner — a person, not a team. Name the verification: a load test, a penetration test, a pseudo-translation pass, an accessibility audit, a privacy review, each with a date that falls before code-complete rather than during release week. And put a review date on the requirement itself, because a target set against 2025's device mix expires quietly.

4 · The arithmeticWhere 2.5 seconds actually goes

Meghana asked Rohit to do something the team had never done: decompose the promise into a budget, hop by hop, in the environment that was actually failing. They fixed the environment first — a 3G connection delivering about 400 kilobits per second of usable throughput with a 180-millisecond round-trip time, an entry-level Android device, the 6 to 9 p.m. peak — and then listed every component of the elapsed time a borrower experiences.

Connection setup, including DNS resolution and the TLS handshake on a cold start, came to roughly 400 milliseconds. Two sequential round trips, one to authenticate and one to fetch, cost 2 × 180 = 360 milliseconds of pure network latency before any bytes of content moved. The API gateway and token validation took about 60 milliseconds. The ledger query that Rohit had been proudly measuring took 240 milliseconds. Rendering the screen on a low-end processor took about 300 milliseconds.

Then the payload. The foreclosure response weighed 180 kilobytes, because it carried the borrower's entire repayment history — every one of up to 36 instalments with its own fee breakdown — plus a base-64 encoded partner-bank logo. At 400 kilobits per second, 180 kilobytes is 1,440 kilobits, which takes 1,440 ÷ 400 = 3.6 seconds to transfer. The transfer alone consumed more than the entire 2.5-second budget, and no amount of database tuning could touch it.

The arithmetic reversed. If the budget is 2,500 milliseconds and the fixed costs are 400 + 360 + 60 + 240 + 300 = 1,360 milliseconds, then transfer may consume 1,140 milliseconds. At 400 kilobits per second that is 456 kilobits, or 57 kilobytes. Rohit rounded down to a 35-kilobyte cap to leave headroom for retries, which meant returning the current payoff quote and the last three instalments rather than all 36, and serving the logo from the app bundle. Design B totalled 2,060 milliseconds — 400 + 360 + 60 + 240 + 700 + 300 — and cleared the budget with room.

Now change one input and watch the requirement change character. Suppose the environment is declared as 4G at 2 megabits per second instead of 3G at 400 kilobits. The original 180-kilobyte payload transfers in 1,440 ÷ 2,000 = 0.72 seconds, and Design A totals about 2,080 milliseconds — it passes. The identical requirement, the identical code, and an opposite verdict. This is the whole lesson of the topic in one line: the environment clause is not context for the number; it is half of the requirement. Ambarish Money had been writing performance requirements against the network conditions of its own office in Kalyani Nagar.

5 · NuancesThe distinctions that separate understanding from vocabulary

The name is wrong, and the wrongness matters

“Non-functional” suggests these requirements are not about behaviour, which is false: latency, availability and audit-trail completeness are all observable behaviour. A useful reading is that functional requirements describe what happens in one interaction while quality requirements describe the distribution of what happens across many interactions and many conditions. That reframing has a practical consequence. You cannot verify an NFR by trying the feature once; you verify it against a population of requests, devices and moments, which is why the verification step is a different activity and usually a different calendar.

A number without a measurement point is decoration

“The screen loads in two seconds” has at least five missing clauses: which screen, on what device and network, at which percentile, measured where, over what observation window. Each omission lets two honest people reach opposite conclusions, as Meghana and Rohit did. The cheapest discipline in this entire topic is to refuse to write a number until all five clauses exist beside it.

Percentiles describe users, not requests

Teams instinctively quote medians because medians look good. But a borrower completing foreclosure makes roughly eight sequential calls, so her chance of meeting a purely independent p95 on every call is 0.95 raised to the eighth power, about 66 per cent — meaning one session in three contains a slow call even when the requirement is met. Jeffrey Dean and Luiz Barroso's 2013 paper on tail latency made the point at scale: as the number of components a request touches grows, the tail becomes the typical experience. Quote p95 and p99, and quote them per user journey, not per endpoint.

Availability composes multiplicatively, not by the weakest link

If the foreclosure journey depends on five services in series, each independently promising 99.9 per cent, the journey's availability is 0.999 to the fifth power, or 99.50 per cent — about 3.6 hours of failure a month rather than 43 minutes. Teams routinely assume the system inherits the target each component promises. It inherits something worse, and the only fixes are redundancy, graceful degradation, or an honest lower number at the top.

Constraints must not be scored, and targets must not be sanctified

Regulatory and contractual requirements — disclosure before consent, storage of payment data within India, retention of security logs — are binary conditions of doing business. Putting them into a prioritisation score alongside features is a category error that eventually produces a spreadsheet in which compliance ranks fourteenth. The converse error is equally expensive: treating a self-chosen performance or availability target as though it were law removes the organisation's ability to trade it, and the trade is usually where the money is.

Every quality has a cost curve with a knee

Availability is the clearest case. Moving from 99.9 to 99.95 per cent halves permitted downtime from 43.2 to 21.6 minutes a month and is typically an operational discipline problem. Moving to 99.99 per cent — 4.32 minutes — usually requires active-active deployment across regions, which changes data architecture, cost and, for an Indian lender with residency obligations, the legal analysis too. Finding the knee, and stopping there, is a product judgement, not an engineering one.

SLI, SLO and SLA are three different objects

A service-level indicator is the measurement — the fraction of foreclosure quote requests returning in under 2.5 seconds. A service-level objective is the internal target for that indicator. A service-level agreement is a contractual promise with a financial consequence. They should not share a number: the SLO should be stricter than the SLA so that missing the objective is a warning rather than an invoice. Teams that conflate them either over-promise to customers or under-alert themselves.

What NFRs cannot tell you

They cannot tell you whether a quality is perceptible. Improving a screen from 900 to 700 milliseconds may be invisible, while 5,000 to 2,000 is transformative; the value of performance work is a step function that the requirement document does not contain. They cannot tell you whether the feature deserves to exist. And a list of security requirements is not a threat model: enumerating controls tells you what you decided to defend, never what an attacker will actually try. The honest edge of this discipline is that NFRs manage known qualities well and unknown adversaries badly.

6 · Where it differsConsumer, B2B, marketplace — and stage

In consumer products such as Ambarish Money, the dominant qualities are those set by the physical world the user inhabits: device class, network quality, battery, data cost, app download size, and language. The binding constraints are rarely in the data centre. Localisation is a genuine non-functional requirement here and is routinely mistaken for a translation task — Devanagari strings typically run 20 to 35 per cent longer than their English equivalents, Indian digit grouping writes ₹12,34,567 where a Western format writes 1,234,567, and a button sized for “Pay now” simply breaks. Meghana's Tier-3 rollout would fail on layout before it failed on meaning.

In business software such as Ambarini Retail Cloud, which sells store-operations software to retail chains, the dominant qualities are contractual and administrative: uptime with service credits, single sign-on, role-based access control, exportability of data, audit trails, and increasingly a customer security questionnaire that functions as a de facto requirements document written by someone else's procurement team. Here NFRs arrive from outside sales conversations and are best captured before the deal, not after.

In marketplaces — a quick-commerce operator such as Ambarvan Fresh, say — the interesting qualities are asymmetric and relational. The demand side cares about latency and accuracy of availability; the supply side cares about consistency and fairness, which produces requirements of a shape consumer products never need, such as a bound on how stale a partner's inventory view may be, or a guarantee that two riders never see the same order as assignable. These are quality requirements about the relationship between users, not about a single user's experience.

Stage changes the economics rather than the concepts. An eight-person company should hold perhaps three explicit non-functional requirements, chosen because violating them would be fatal or illegal, and should consciously accept debt everywhere else. A company at Ambarish Money's scale has a different problem: its NFRs are the only thing keeping a shared platform habitable for eleven teams, which means they must be owned centrally, budgeted, and enforced in the build pipeline rather than in a document.

7 · Common mistakesSymptom, cause, diagnostic

The boilerplate annex

The symptom is visible from outside: every PRD in the organisation contains the same four sentences about performance, security, scale and compliance. The underlying misunderstanding is that non-functional requirements are a document section to be completed rather than a set of feature-specific choices. The cheapest diagnostic is one question in review: which of these would have stopped us shipping last quarter's release? If the answer is none, the section is decoration, and the honest move is to delete it and write two real scenarios instead.

Copying the most impressive number

The symptom is a PRD promising 99.99 per cent availability and 200-millisecond response times in a company whose on-call rotation has four people and whose largest customer contract specifies 99.5 per cent. The misunderstanding is that a target is an expression of ambition rather than a purchased commitment. The diagnostic is to ask engineering for the marginal cost of the last nine — the incremental infrastructure and staffing required to move from 99.9 to 99.99. If nobody can produce a figure, the number was never real.

Verifying qualities in release week

The symptom is a project plan in which the load test, the penetration test and the privacy review all appear after code-complete. The misunderstanding is that quality attributes are properties you inspect for, like typos, rather than properties you architect for. The diagnostic is purely calendrical: open the plan and look for a security or performance activity dated before the first line of production code. Its absence predicts rework with uncomfortable reliability.

Compliance by screenshot

The symptom is a team that believes consent is handled because there is a checkbox on a screen. The misunderstanding is confusing the user interface for a legal obligation with the record-keeping and revocation machinery that the obligation actually requires. The diagnostic is a single trace: ask to be shown, end to end, what happens in every system when one named borrower withdraws consent — which records are deleted, which are retained and under what legal basis, and who can prove it eleven months later.

8 · What good looks like

Handled well, this is not a longer PRD section; it is a shorter and sharper one. Meghana's revised artefact ran to a single page per feature, and the foreclosure page carried five scenarios, one of which is reproduced below in the Planguage-style form Gilb proposed: a scale, a meter, a must, a plan, an owner and a verification date.

Five such scenarios covered performance, availability, disclosure, data residency and localisation. Nothing else was written down.

Two features of that artefact matter more than its format. First, every line can be failed, which is what makes it a requirement. Second, one tradeoff is recorded explicitly rather than discovered later: showing three instalments instead of 36 is a real loss of information, accepted deliberately in exchange for the screen loading at all, with a note that the full history remains one tap away.

9 · The decision

Meghana's decision, taken on 12 March 2026, was to delete the four boilerplate sentences from the PRD template altogether and replace them with a rule: no feature enters development without between three and six quality scenarios, each with a meter and an owner, and none may be copied from a previous PRD. She set the foreclosure target at 2,500 milliseconds rather than the 1,800 the design team wanted, on the reasoning that 1,800 would have required an offline cache of loan state on the device — an eight-week project with a genuine data-protection question attached — while 2,500 required a payload cap she could ship in nine days. She committed 99.95 per cent availability internally against a 99.5 per cent contractual figure, and she declined to chase 99.99.

The reasoning is worth separating from the numbers. Meghana treated the two regulatory constraints as design inputs and the two performance targets as purchases, priced them, and bought the cheaper one first. She did not improve quality; she made quality arguable, which is the precondition for improving it.

What to learn next follows directly. Compliance and audit requirements takes the lower half of the map in section three and treats it properly, because constraints imposed by regulation have their own evidentiary machinery — records, retention, reportability — that a target-shaped requirement cannot express. Release criteria and success metrics closes the loop by deciding which of these promises actually gates a launch. And acceptance criteria and error cases is where the feature-local half of this discipline gets written into the stories developers pick up on a Monday morning.

Two questions to sit with. First: take the last requirement document you wrote and find the one quality claim in it that you could not fail — what number, measurement point and environment would you have had to add to make failure possible, and would anyone have agreed to it? Second: in your product, which quality is currently a target that everybody treats as a constraint, and which is a constraint that everybody treats as a target — and what has each mistake cost you so far?

Nammane Pay: Autopay and the Four Things It Must Also Be

1. Opening

Tuesday 6 October 2026, 7.40 a.m. In a glass-walled room in Bengaluru's Indiranagar, Aswathy Haridasan, head of product at Nammane Pay, pinned a one-page scope note to the wall and counted what it listed. Autopay for society maintenance dues was due to go live on Tuesday 1 December, when up to 288,000 paying flats could meet the month with an automatic debit instead of a reminder; the forecast is 86,400. Her squad had twelve engineer-weeks of feature work committed. It also owed the feature four things no resident would ask for by name: speed under load, India-only storage of payment data, a record of each resident's consent, and screens residents could read in their own language. By 5 p.m. on Friday 9 October she had to tell the sponsor bank's certification desk what would ship on 1 December. The build began on Monday 12 October, and the bank booked its slots on what it was told.

2. Company background

Nammane Pay was founded in Bengaluru in 2019 by two former bankers who had watched treasurers chase maintenance dues over WhatsApp. It collects monthly dues for 2,400 housing societies in Bengaluru, Pune, Hyderabad and Chennai over UPI, and earns a flat ₹9 on each payment. In September 2026, 288,000 flats paid through it. It began with 14 Bengaluru societies, reached Pune in 2021, Hyderabad in 2022 and Chennai in 2024. Some 140 people work for the company; the payments squad has five engineers, two in Bengaluru and three in Pune.

The field is crowded. MyGate and NoBrokerHood bundle dues collection with gate and visitor management, ApnaComplex serves treasurers with accounting, and PhonePe and CRED let a resident pay a society bill from a general-purpose app. Nammane's wedge is reconciliation: each payment lands against the right flat in the treasurer's ledger. Its payments run on rails operated by NPCI, through a private-sector sponsor bank whose certification any new mandate product must clear.

3. The situation

Autopay lets a resident authorise a recurring UPI mandate once; Nammane then debits the dues at 6 a.m. on the 1st. The bank's August trial, with eleven societies, showed that it releases debits in tranches, and its busiest minute carried 3.0 times the average rate of the two-hour window from 6 to 8 a.m. Exhibit 1 turns the forecast into volume: 86,400 debits, which is 12.0 a second on average (86,400 ÷ 7,200 s) and 36.0 a second in the busiest minute. On Thursday 1 October, manual payments had peaked at 41,760 in the same window, 5.8 a second.

Exhibit 2 gives the squad's load test of Monday 28 September. The platform meets its own targets, a p95 confirmation time of 3 seconds and a p99 of 8 seconds, at 14 a second and misses them at 24. Nothing was run above 24. If both targets hold, at most 5 per cent of debits (4,320 of 86,400) may take over 3 seconds and at most 1 per cent (864) over 8 seconds; these are ceilings, and they apply only if the targets are met.

A memo from the general counsel, dated Friday 2 October, adds two points. The DPDP Rules, notified in November 2025, bring most duties into force around May 2027. The RBI's 2018 directive that payment-system data be stored only in India applies today, and customer-success tickets exported to Nammane's Singapore-hosted help desk carry residents' UPI IDs. The Act also entitles a resident to read a consent request in English or any language of the Constitution's Eighth Schedule. The Berlin-based designer has drafted the mandate screen in Kannada, Marathi, Telugu and Tamil. The customer-success lead in Singapore, whose team runs the help desk, reports that Chennai treasurers already forward Tamil WhatsApp messages asking what a "mandate" is. Exhibit 3 prices each requirement in engineer-weeks, and Figure 1 lays out the calendar.

4. The people

Aswathy Haridasan, head of product, Bengaluru. She owns the scope note and the bank relationship. She wants to ship something safe for residents on 1 December and to defend every omission to the bank, to her chief executive and to the treasurers.

Achutan Heggade, engineering lead, Pune. He wants capacity spent where the platform has no evidence of coping. His estimates are in Exhibit 3, and he will not certify a launch whose load he has not tested.

8. A note for the learner

A non-functional requirement states a quality the feature must also have. It rarely appears in a customer request, yet it decides whether the feature can ship. A useful first move is to classify each by what follows from missing it: a gate, where the law or the bank blocks you; a threshold, where the feature works up to a load and then fails; or a quality, where users drift away. The same requirement can be a gate for one feature and a quality for another, so the classification belongs to the case, not to the topic. Then price each in one unit against the capacity the calendar truly leaves.

One defensible path is Option C. Performance is a threshold with no evidence above 24 a second, so it ships. India-only storage is a gate under a directive already in force, so it ships. Localisation behaves as a gate too: residents may read consent in an Eighth Schedule language, and 60 per cent of Chennai's tickets are regional, so an English-only mandate invites consent that is hard to defend. The ledger's duty falls near May 2027, so it follows in January with a date attached. Because C leaves no contingency, Achutan might spread debits over six hours: 86,400 ÷ 21,600 s is 4.0 a second, and 12.0 in the busiest minute at 3.0 times if that factor carries over from the two-hour release, under the 14 tested. That could trim the nine performance weeks by an amount he has yet to estimate. The path changes if the bank makes the ledger a certification condition: then A or B replaces C.

2. Pathivu Technologies, 2014 to 2026

Balagopal Iringal and two colleagues from a payments processor started Pathivu in Bengaluru in 2014. Its first product, Pathivu Core, reconciled an NBFC's day of field collections against its bank statements overnight. Core was a batch system; a run that finished by six in the morning was a good run. In January 2024 the company launched Pathivu Stream, a real-time settlement-confirmation API built on Core's existing ledger tables. It was sold as real time, and still measured the way Core had been.

3. The industry

India's payments stack made Pathivu's market and set its clock. UPI, run by NPCI, taught merchants to expect confirmation in the time it takes to look up from a phone; Zerodha and Groww did the same for retail investors. The Reserve Bank's April 2018 directive on storage of payment system data requires payment data to be held only in India. The Digital Personal Data Protection Act of 2023 put consent and erasure on the backlog, and GST e-invoicing, ONDC and the account aggregator framework each added an interface that had to be fast and auditable at once.

Pathivu competed from the middle. Above it sat the core-banking suites of TCS and Infosys; beside it, Razorpay, Cashfree, Juspay and Perfios had built capability a client might licence instead; below it, any marketplace of size could build its own. Festival peaks set by Flipkart, Meesho and Zepto define a sale weekend, and Puthukada Retail, with 180 million registered users and an RBI-licensed payment aggregator of its own, intended to be in that company.
